story: In 1985, Soviet cosmonaut Vladimir Dzhanibekov was on a mission to the Salyut 7 space station when he noticed something bizarre. A spinning object in zero gravity did not just rotate; it spontaneously and repeatedly flipped 180 degrees back and forth without any external force. This mind-bending phenomenon is known as the Dzhanibekov effect or the tennis racket theorem. Though mathematically described by Louis Poinsot in 1834, Dzhanibekov's orbital discovery stunned observers. The math shows that rotating a rigid body around its intermediate axis of inertia is highly unstable, causing even a tiny disturbance to trigger a flip. This law of physics has major real-world consequences: it caused America's first satellite, Explorer 1, to wobble out of control in 1958, and nearly destroyed the joint NASA-ESA Solar and Heliospheric Observatory in 1998. You can even test it yourself by safely tossing your smartphone in the air!
angle: A spinning asymmetrical object in the weightlessness of space will spontaneously and repeatedly flip 180 degrees back and forth on its own, a bizarre physical law that nearly destroyed a multi-million dollar NASA spacecraft.
disputed: The sources disagree on how Dzhanibekov observed the effect and what object he used. S2 states he observed it while unscrewing a wingnut used to lock down supplies from Earth. S3 states he turned a wrench out of frustration while filming a spacewalk and let it float away. The script should avoid mentioning the frustration and spacewalk details, and instead describe it broadly as a spinning metal tool or nut unscrewed in microgravity.
